questions.stem: This question asks the reader to use “Identify the hidden premise in a clinical prevention argument / What must be equal for cost to decide? / Hidden premise”. Which option results?

options.misconception: reverses the direction of the reasoning the passage sets out
selects "All prevention works" where the rule in the passage requires a different condition

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: the core hidden premise is that cheaper prevention is equally effective. On that basis "Cheaper prevention is equally effective" is the supported choice. Option A ("Cost is irrelevant") fails because it opposite of the text; Option B ("Prevention is always free") fails because it reverses the direction of the reasoning that settles hidden premise; Option C ("All prevention works") fails because it selects "All prevention works" where hidden premise requires a different condition.
questions.hint: What must be equal for cost to decide?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a counterargument addresses the claim's evidence

stimulus.body: A note claims a therapy works based on 10 trials. A reviewer replies that 8 of the 10 trials were industry-funded.

questions.stem: A note claims a therapy works based on 10 trials. A reviewer replies that 8 of the 10 trials were industry-funded. Does the counterargument engage the claim?

options.text: Yes, because industry is always biased.
Yes, because funding source may bias results.

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: funding source may bias results, so the counterargument engages the evidence. On that basis "Yes, because funding source may bias results" is the supported choice. Option A ("Yes, because industry is always biased") fails because it overstates to always; Option B ("No, because funding is irrelevant") fails because it dismisses a relevant concern; Option D ("No, because trials are useless") fails because it rejects trials wholesale.
questions.hint: Does funding affect evidence quality?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a note introduces an irrelevant ethical point

stimulus.body: Read this source excerpt carefully: «It introduces a red herring.» Shifting to animal-testing ethics distracts from efficacy. A marginal reminder adds: does ethics address efficacy. It is followed by four candidate interpretations, of which exactly one is supported by the wording of the excerpt.

questions.stem: The excerpt is judged by “Identify when a note introduces an irrelevant ethical point / Does ethics address efficacy? / Red herring”. Which answer is the warranted one?
questions.explanation: Close reading of the note yields this rule: shifting to animal-testing ethics distracts from efficacy. On that basis "It introduces a red herring" is the supported choice. Option A ("It defines efficacy") fails because it confuses distraction with definition; Option B ("It strengthens the efficacy claim") fails because it confuses distraction with support; Option C ("It retracts the efficacy claim") fails because it reads shift as retraction.
questions.hint: Does ethics address efficacy?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a clinician's note should not overstate limited findings

stimulus.body: A short reference note on insufficient evidence is set for a close-reading task. It states: Overstating evidence misleads and risks harm. A marginal reminder adds: what happens if the cure claim is wrong. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: The standard for this item is “Explain why a clinician's note should not overstate limited findings / What happens if the cure claim is wrong? / Insufficient…”. Which option meets the standard?

answer.exemplar: Overstating tentative findings as cures misleads readers and clinicians, risking harmful decisions and eroding trust when results fail to replicate.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: overstating evidence misleads and risks harm. On that basis "Overstating tentative findings as cures misleads readers and clinicians, risking harmful…" is the supported choice.
questions.hint: What happens if the cure claim is wrong?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Analyze whether a note's rebuttal is proportional to the objection

stimulus.body: A note concedes a drug has a 0.1 percent rash risk, then writes three pages defending against it. a 0.1 percent risk does not warrant three pages. A marginal reminder adds: compare response length to risk size. Four statements are offered, and only one follows from the note.

questions.stem: The check to perform is “Analyze whether a note's rebuttal is proportional to the objection / Compare response length to risk size. / Meeting a…”. Which option passes that check?

options.text: Yes, because any risk needs full defence.
No, because the response exceeds the risk magnitude.
No, because rebuttals are never useful.

questions.explanation: What settles the item is the relation stated in the passage: a 0.1 percent risk does not warrant three pages. On that basis "No, because the response exceeds the risk magnitude" is the supported choice. Option A ("Yes, because any risk needs full defence") fails because it confuses thoroughness with proportion; Option B ("Yes, because rashes are serious") fails because it overstates the risk; Option D ("No, because rebuttals are never useful") fails because it rejects rebuttals wholesale.
questions.hint: Compare response length to risk size.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a note cites irrelevant personal experience

stimulus.body: A note claims a drug works, citing the author's personal use.

questions.stem: A note claims a drug works, citing the author's personal use. Is the cited evidence relevant?

options.text: Yes, because personal use shows efficacy.
No, because personal experience is always false.
Yes, because the author is credible.
No, because personal experience is not clinical evidence.

questions.explanation: Close reading of the note yields this rule: personal use is not clinical evidence. On that basis "No, because personal experience is not clinical evidence" is the supported choice. Option A ("Yes, because personal use shows efficacy") fails because it confuses anecdote with evidence; Option B ("No, because personal experience is always false") fails because it rejects personal experience wholesale; Option C ("Yes, because the author is credible") fails because it appeals to author credibility.
questions.hint: Does personal use measure efficacy?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumed warrant in a clinical screening argument

stimulus.body: A short reference note on assumed warrants is set for a close-reading task. It states: The core hidden warrant equates a positive test with disease presence. A marginal reminder adds: what must be true for the conclusion to follow. Four statements are then offered, and only one of them follows from what the note actually says.

questions.stem: A reviewer is weighing competing claims about assumed warrants, among them "The test is always accurate". Based only on the excerpt above, which answer is the one the evidence warrants?

options.text: A positive test always means disease.

questions.explanation: The passage gives the controlling distinction: the core hidden warrant equates a positive test with disease presence. On that basis "A positive test always means disease" is the supported choice. Option A ("The patient wants testing") fails because it different assumption; Option B ("The test is always accurate") fails because it different assumption, less central; Option D ("The disease is curable") fails because it different assumption.
questions.hint: What must be true for the conclusion to follow?
